headline: Ocean's humped up — the real bite moved inside the inlet
subhead: With a three-foot swell hammering the beach, the smart money is working Sloop Channel, the bay flats, and the rocks on the drop — not the open sand.
body_markdown:
_AI fishing-intelligence report. It was prepared from 0 supplied evidence records and 17 supplied analysis inputs; it does not claim firsthand fishing._

Everybody and their brother is still parking at Field 6 and bombing bunker chunks into the surf off Jones Beach like it's October. I get it — muscle memory, that big-fish dream. But with the ocean running 3.6 feet at 6 seconds and no sign of laying down, that's a young man's game right now, and a frustrating one. I've been steering people toward Sloop Channel, the bay flats off Short Beach, and the rock piles at the inlet mouth, because that's where the fish actually are this week — and where the tide is doing the work for you instead of against you.

Here's the read. Buoy data off the coast is showing 75.9°F water and a beat-up sea state, while the back bay and inlet channels are running warmer and calmer under that August sun. That thermal split matters. Bait and predators alike don't want to fight three-foot slop and a steep gradient — they're stacking in the protected water where the current is manageable and the forage is concentrated. Every guy grinding the open beach for four hours with nothing to show for it is fishing against the grain. The fish moved into the house. Go find them there.

Fluke first, because that's still the bread-and-butter through mid-August. Sloop Channel is holding fish in 20 to 28 feet on the drift, and the pattern hasn't changed — white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last two hours of the outgoing. Add a squid strip if the bite's finicky. Fish are running mixed sizes, plenty of shorts mixed with keepers to 4-5 pounds, so cover water and don't marry one drift. The channel edges near the deeper humps are where the better fish have been coming from — not the flat middle.

Weakfish are the story nobody's talking about enough, and they should be. South Oyster Bay's mud-bottom stretches, especially the deeper holes off Short Beach, have been giving up legal weakfish on the evening tide — that hour before dark into the start of the ebb. Small bucktails, quarter-ounce, tipped with a thin strip of squid or a 3-inch chartreuse soft plastic, worked with a slow lift-and-drop right off bottom. These fish have been scarce for a decade in this bay, so treat every one with respect — handle them gently, they're notoriously soft-mouthed and don't survive rough treatment if you're releasing.

Now the bluefish. We flagged this pattern a few days back — said wherever bunker pods concentrate you'd get violent topwater feeds as long as the calm high pressure held and the bunker stayed thick. That's exactly what's playing out at the inlet mouth and along the flats off Short Beach. When a bunker school gets pinned up against the flats on the last of the incoming, the blues turn it into total chaos — poppers, Hopkins, anything that throws a commotion on top. Doesn't last long, maybe 20 minutes before the school scatters, so when you see the birds diving and the surface nervous, don't wait — get on it.

Stripers are still around the inlet rocks and the jetty at Jones, but the pattern's a night bite right now with the ocean this stirred up. Outgoing tide, dusk into the dark hours, is when the current rips past the rocks hardest and bass slide up to ambush bait getting swept out of the bay. Live bunker on a fish-finder rig fished tight to the rock structure, or a bucktail worked along the current seam if you want to stay mobile. Worth noting — Field 1 at the east end has expanded night access this year, Friday through Sunday, dusk to 6am, if you've got the Night Sport Fishing Permit and the DEC registry squared away. That's a legit option for guys who want a shot at bass after the ocean beach empties out and don't want to fight the jetty crowd.

Porgies are filling in around the rock piles at the inlet and under the Wantagh Bridge on bottom rigs with bloodworms or clam — steady, unspectacular, good for a mixed bag or if you're breaking in a kid on rod-and-reel basics. Blackfish are still a month-plus away; don't waste bloodworms on them yet.

Look ahead: if this swell holds through the weekend, keep the ocean beach as a backup plan and lean on the inlet and bay pattern — it's produced steadier fish for less abuse. If the wind finally swings out of the northwest and the ocean lays down, I'd expect some of that bass and blue activity to redistribute back toward the open beach and the jetty tips at first light. Watch the bunker — where they go, the bluefish and the bigger bass follow. That's been true all summer, and nothing in this week's conditions says it's about to change.
